title: Exams and exam season
introHtml:
If the term went well, exam season is mostly about practice under exam conditions rather than learning new material. The ratio shifts towards questions and past papers.

A useful picture: during the term you build the knowledge; in exam season you practise getting it out, fast, in the exact shape the exam asks for. Memory works best when the way you practise matches the way you will be tested (researchers call this transfer-appropriate processing). Someone who has only read about swimming is not ready for a race, however many books they read. This applies to a school final, a university exam, a bar exam, a driving theory test, a language certificate or a coding interview.

items.title: Start practice questions early
items.leadHtml: Start from the first weeks of the term, not the last two.

parts.why: Answering questions is not only a way to measure learning; it is one of the strongest ways to produce it (the testing effect). Students who test themselves remember far more a week later than students who reread the same material, even though rereading feels more productive at the time. Starting early also spreads the questions out, so you get the spacing benefit for free, and you discover your misunderstandings while there is still time to fix them.
parts.how:
1. After each week's lessons, do a small set of questions (5 to 15) on that week plus a few older topics.
  2. Read the explanation for every question you got wrong or guessed.
  3. Do not save the question bank or past papers "for later so they stay fresh". A fresh bank you never use is worth nothing.

examples.simple: a school student does the end-of-chapter questions in the geography textbook on the day the chapter is finished, not in the revision week.
examples.nontrivial: a law student uses past exam problem questions from week three, even though she can only answer a third of each one. Writing a partial answer tells her which rules she cannot yet apply, which no amount of reading would show.
examples.html:
• Simple: a school student does the end-of-chapter questions in the geography textbook on the day the chapter is finished, not in the revision week.
  • Non-trivial: a law student uses past exam problem questions from week three, even though she can only answer a third of each one. Writing a partial answer tells her which rules she cannot yet apply, which no amount of reading would show.

parts.time: One exam-style question with its explanation is ~2-3 min (~4-6×). Still one of the best uses of study time.

reading.html: What is retrieval practice?, Pooja Agarwal, RetrievalPractice.org

reading.label: Paper
reading.html: Roediger & Karpicke (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science.

items.title: Past papers and question banks
items.leadHtml: These are the best predictor of exam content. Notice what kinds of questions keep coming up.

parts.why: Examiners are people with habits. The same course is usually examined by the same people, with the same favourite topics, question shapes and command words ("compare", "evaluate", "derive"). Past papers show you the target you are actually aiming at, not the whole syllabus in equal weight.
parts.how:
1. Collect several years of past papers (from the course page, the department, the exam board or older students).
  2. Tally the topics and question types across years. A simple table is enough.
  3. Do at least one recent paper early to see the level, and keep the most recent ones for timed mocks near the end.
  4. Use question banks for volume and past papers for realism.

examples.simple: a student tallying five years of chemistry papers sees that a titration calculation appears every year, and makes sure she can do one in her sleep.
examples.nontrivial: a history student notices that the essay questions never ask "describe" but always "how far" or "to what extent". He stops memorising narratives and starts practising arguments with a judgement in the first paragraph.

items.title: Simulate the exam
items.leadHtml: Use the same time limit, no notes, and the same time of day if possible. Do at least one full mock.

parts.why: An exam tests more than knowledge: it tests pacing, stamina, handling pressure and recalling without any cues. Each of those can be practised. A full mock shows whether you run out of time, where your concentration dips (often in the third hour), and which question types make you freeze. It also makes the real exam feel familiar, which lowers anxiety.
parts.how:
1. Pick a past paper you have not seen.
  2. Set a timer for the real duration, sit at a desk, phone away, no notes.
  3. Mark it honestly using the mark scheme, then fill in your error log.
  4. Check your timing per question: where did you lose minutes?

examples.simple: a student taking a language listening exam does a full past listening paper with the audio played once only, as in the real exam, not with pauses.
examples.nontrivial: a candidate for a 4-hour professional accounting exam does a full mock on a Saturday morning at 9 am and discovers that his accuracy drops sharply after hour three. He changes his order of attack (long questions first while fresh) and practises a 2-minute reset routine between sections.
examples.html:
• Simple: a student taking a language listening exam does a full past listening paper with the audio played once only, as in the real exam, not with pauses.
  • Non-trivial: a candidate for a 4-hour professional accounting exam does a full mock on a Saturday morning at 9 am and discovers that his accuracy drops sharply after hour three. He changes his order of attack (long questions first while fresh) and practises a 2-minute reset routine between sections.

parts.time: The length of the exam plus about the same again for marking and analysis. Worth it 1 to 3 times per major exam.

items.title: Error log
items.leadHtml: For every wrong answer, note the topic, why you got it wrong (did not know it, misread the question, confused it with something else, ran out of time) and the fix.

parts.why: A wrong answer is the most valuable thing a practice session produces, but only if you learn from it. Errors that you notice and correct, especially ones you made with high confidence, tend to be remembered very well afterwards (Metcalfe 2017). Logging the type of error also reveals patterns that a score alone hides: you might not have a knowledge problem at all, but a reading-the-question problem.
parts.how:
Keep a simple table:

Question / topicWhat I answeredCorrect answerError typeFix
Stats: p-value interpretation"Probability H0 is true"Probability of data this extreme if H0 trueMisconceptionCard + explain to a friend
Physics Q7Units in cmShould be mCarelessAlways write units in the first line

Review the log weekly, and redo the logged questions a few days later without looking at the answer.

examples.simple: a maths student sees that 6 of her last 10 errors were sign mistakes, not concept errors, and adds a 30-second check of signs before moving on.
examples.nontrivial: a medical student's log shows she keeps confusing two similar conditions. Instead of more single facts, she makes a comparison table of the two and practises mixed questions on both. The pair stops appearing in her log.

items.title: Weak topics first
items.leadHtml: Use question-bank statistics or your error log to choose what to review.

parts.why: It is pleasant to revise what you already know, because it feels fluent and reassuring. But a point gained on a weak topic counts exactly the same as a point on a strong one, and is much easier to win. Students left to themselves tend to reread rather than test, and so they misjudge what they know (Karpicke, Butler & Roediger 2009). Data from questions corrects that illusion.
parts.how:
1. Sort your topics by score (question bank stats, mock results or error log counts).
  2. Spend most revision time on the bottom third, but keep light reviews of strong topics so they do not fade.
  3. Re-test each weak topic after working on it to check it actually moved.

examples.simple: a driving theory candidate scores 95% on road signs and 60% on stopping distances, so she spends her evening on stopping distances.
examples.nontrivial: an economics student finds his weakest topic is also the least examined. He gives it a modest share of time and spends more on the second-weakest topic, which appears every year. Weakness times weight, not weakness alone, decides the order.

items.title: Interleave in the final weeks
items.leadHtml: Mix courses and topics, the way the exam will.

parts.why: In a chapter's exercises, you always know which method to use: it is the one from the chapter. In an exam, the hardest part is often recognising which kind of problem you are looking at. Mixing problem types forces you to practise exactly that choice. In one classic study, students who practised mixed maths problems did far better on a later test than students who practised in blocks, even though blocked practice felt easier at the time (Rohrer & Taylor 2007).
parts.how:
1. Build question sets that mix topics from across the course in random order.
  2. Before solving each one, name the topic or method ("this is a conservation of energy problem").
  3. Expect it to feel slower and harder; that is the point.

examples.simple: a language learner mixes past, present and future tense exercises in one set, instead of a page of each.
examples.nontrivial: a programmer preparing for coding interviews shuffles problems from arrays, graphs, dynamic programming and strings, and gives himself two minutes to decide the approach before writing code. His weak point turns out to be spotting when a problem is a graph problem in disguise, something blocked practice never revealed.

parts.time: ~1× extra: it changes the order, not the amount, though it feels ~20-30% slower.

items.title: Know the format
items.leadHtml: Every exam format needs its own practice: multiple-choice questions (MCQs), short answers, essays, problem sets, oral exams, practical exams and speaking tests.

parts.why: Knowing something and producing it in a particular format are different skills. Recognising the right option among five is easier than writing it from nothing; writing it is different from saying it aloud to an examiner; saying it is different from doing it with your hands. Memory is most accessible when practice and test use the same kind of processing (Morris, Bransford & Franks 1977), so practise in the format you will face.
parts.how:
Find out the format, the marking scheme and the timing, then practise that exact thing:

  • MCQs: lots of timed questions; practise eliminating wrong options.
  • Short answers: answer from a blank page in the word limit; compare with the mark scheme's key points.
  • Essays: practise planning a thesis and structure in 5 to 10 minutes, and write some full timed essays.
  • Problem sets (maths, physics, economics): solve unseen problems with full working; marks often come from the method.
  • Oral exams and vivas: explain topics aloud to a partner who interrupts with questions.
  • Practical exams: rehearse the actual actions with a checklist, aloud, with a partner timing you. In medicine these are OSCEs (timed clinical stations); in science they may be lab practicals; in music, auditions.
  • Coding interviews: solve problems while talking through your reasoning, on a whiteboard or a plain editor without autocomplete.
  • Language speaking exams: record yourself answering typical prompts for 2 minutes, then listen back.

examples.simple: a student with an open-book exam practises finding things fast in her book (tabs, an index page), because looking things up eats the time.
examples.nontrivial: a philosophy student who writes excellent essays at home freezes in his first oral exam. For the next one he practises with a friend who asks "but why?" after each sentence, and learns to give short answers with one example instead of long monologues.

items.title: No new resources in the last week

parts.why: A new book or video series in the last week feels like progress but mostly brings new terminology, new framing and new gaps you will not have time to close. It also eats time that should go to retrieval and mocks. Worse, it can unsettle what you know ("this book says it differently, which is right?"). In the final week, consolidation beats expansion.
parts.how:
1. Before the final week, decide your final set of materials: your notes, your cards, your error log, and past papers.
  2. Allow one exception: a targeted look-up to fix a specific error.
  3. Spend the week on recall, mixed questions and one more mock.

examples.simple: a student who discovers a popular revision video series five days before the exam adds it to a list "for next year" and keeps going with her own cards.
examples.nontrivial: a certification candidate realises a whole topic is missing from his notes. Instead of starting a new 10-hour course, he reads the official exam guide section on it once, makes 10 cards and does 20 questions. Accepting a partly covered topic is better than sacrificing everything else.

items.title: Protect sleep before the exam
items.leadHtml: Sleep matters more than one more late-night session.

parts.why: During sleep, the brain replays and stabilises what you learned during the day, so sleep is part of studying, not a break from it (Diekelmann & Born 2010). Sleep loss also hurts exactly what exams need: attention, working memory and reasoning. A study of university chemistry students found that sleep over the weeks before a test was linked to their grades, while sleep on the single night before was not (Okano et al. 2019). The lesson is double: one good night will not rescue a month of bad sleep, and one all-nighter throws away memories you built.
parts.how:
1. In exam season, keep regular sleep and wake times, also at weekends.
  2. Stop studying at least an hour before bed; the last-minute extra is worth less than the sleep it costs.
  3. Caffeine early in the day only.
  4. If you cannot sleep the night before, rest anyway and do not panic: one poor night has less effect than people fear.

examples.simple: a school student stops revising at 21:30 the night before her biology exam and does a 10-minute card review in the morning instead.
examples.nontrivial: a student with exams on consecutive days resists the urge to study until 2 am for the second one. He does a short recall session after the first exam, sleeps normally, and uses the morning for a quick mixed review. His second exam goes better than the first, the opposite of last year.

  • Non-trivial: a student with exams on consecutive days resists the urge to study until 2 am for the second one. items.title: Calm exam-day nerves
items.leadHtml: Some nervousness helps; too much blocks memory. A few simple routines keep it in the helpful range.

parts.why: Anxiety uses up working memory: part of your mind is busy worrying, so less is left for the question. Two short interventions have good evidence. Writing about your worries for about 10 minutes before an exam improved test scores for anxious students, apparently by offloading the worry onto paper (Ramirez & Beilock 2011). items.bodyHtml:
Some nervousness helps; too much blocks memory. A few simple routines keep it in the helpful range.

Why it works. Anxiety uses up working memory: part of your mind is busy worrying, so less is left for the question. Two short interventions have good evidence. Writing about your worries for about 10 minutes before an exam improved test scores for anxious students, apparently by offloading the worry onto paper (Ramirez & Beilock 2011). Telling yourself that a racing heart is your body preparing to perform, rather than a sign of danger, improved maths scores in students preparing for a graduate admissions test (Jamieson and colleagues). And the best long-term cure is regular low-stakes testing all term: in one large classroom study most students said quizzes made them less anxious about exams (Agarwal et al. 2014).

How to do it.

  1. All term: frequent, low-stakes self-testing, so tests become routine.
  2. Before the exam: 5 to 10 minutes of writing down your worries, then put the paper away.
  3. At the desk: a few slow breaths with a long exhale; say "this is energy, not danger".
  4. If you blank on a question: move on, and let your mind work on it in the background.

Examples.

  • Simple: a student who always panics in maths tests writes "I'm worried I'll forget the formulas and fail" in the corridor, then feels calmer going in.
  • Non-trivial: a language learner dreads the speaking part of her exam. She practises with recorded mock interviews weekly for a month. By exam day the format is boring rather than frightening, and her nerves are about the content, not the situation.

items.title: During the exam
items.leadHtml: Read each question carefully and know what it is asking before you answer, move on from hard questions and come back at the end.

parts.why: In an exam, time is the scarcest resource, and it is easy to sink ten minutes into one hard question while three easy ones go unanswered. Marks are usually equal per question type, so collect the easy ones first. Coming back later also helps: a fresh look, or a cue from another question, often unlocks what was stuck. And contrary to the popular advice "never change your first answer", studies show that changed answers more often go from wrong to right; people remember the painful wrong changes more vividly (Kruger, Wirtz & Miller 2005).
parts.how:
Start with a quick look at the whole paper and divide your time by the marks. Then, by format:

  • MCQs: for long case-based questions, read the last line (the actual question) first, then the stem with that in mind. Eliminate wrong options. Flag and move on, then come back.
  • Essays: spend 5 to 10 minutes planning: thesis, 3 or 4 points, evidence for each. A planned essay that is shorter beats an unplanned one that wanders.
  • Maths and science problems: do the problems you can do first. Show your working, because method marks count even when the final answer is wrong.
  • Orals and speaking exams: pause before answering; it is fine to say "let me think for a moment". Structure your answer: point, example, conclusion.
  • Practicals: follow your rehearsed checklist and say what you are doing.
  • All formats: leave 5 to 10 minutes to check, and change an answer when you have a clear reason, not just a vague doubt.

examples.simple: a student in a 2-hour physics exam skips a nasty question 3, finishes 4 to 8, then returns to 3 with 25 minutes left and solves part of it.
examples.nontrivial: a history student plans her essay for 8 minutes while classmates start writing at once. Her plan reveals that her best evidence fits a different argument than her first idea, and she changes her thesis before writing a word, instead of halfway through.

items.title: After the exam
items.leadHtml: Note what surprised you and adjust your method for the next block.

parts.why: Most students look at the grade and move on, which wastes the most honest feedback they will ever get on their study method. A short reflection while the exam is fresh shows whether your preparation matched what was asked. Many universities use "exam wrappers", short reflection sheets after each exam, for exactly this reason: students who reflect on how they prepared tend to change their strategy, not just their effort.
parts.how:
Within a day or two, write answers to:

  1. What surprised me (topics, format, difficulty, timing)?
  2. Where did I lose marks: knowledge, misreading, time, nerves?
  3. Which preparation helped most, and which was wasted?
  4. What one thing will I change for the next exam?

When results or feedback arrive, add the details to your error log.

examples.simple: "Surprised by how many graph questions there were. Next time: practise graphs from week 1."
examples.nontrivial: a nursing student realises she knew the content but lost marks because her short answers missed the key terms in the marking scheme. For the next module she practises writing answers against mark schemes, and her score rises without any extra study hours.
